title: Asalha again
hook: the first sermon, heard a fourth year

segments.voice: Yesterday, Poson, and a tracker following footprints. Your line was who brought it. Did a thank-you go out to someone who carried something to you? Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.

How does a sermon end? Usually, people stand up and go home. The first sermon ends differently. In the Deer Park near Benares, the Buddha finishes speaking to five ascetics, and the sutta turns its camera upward. The gods of the earth hear it and shout: the wheel has been set rolling, and nobody in the world can turn it back. The gods above them hear the shout and pass it on, and the gods above them, heaven after heaven, all the way up. The whole world system trembles, and a great light appears. You've heard this sermon on Asalha's full moon before: the middle way, the four truths. This fourth time, listen for something quieter inside it, a pattern that makes it easy to carry home.
screen: `A SERMON IN THE DEER PARK.` → `THE SHOUT GOES UP.` → `A PATTERN INSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the four truths, short. There is suffering. It has a cause, craving. It can end. And there's a path to its ending. Second, the pattern. In the sutta, the Buddha doesn't just name each truth. He walks around each one three times. This is suffering. Suffering is to be fully understood. Suffering has been fully understood. Then the cause: this is the cause; it is to be let go; it has been let go. Then the ending: this is the ending; it is to be seen for yourself; it has been seen. Then the path: this is the path; it is to be walked; it has been walked. Each truth gets a different job. One to understand, one to let go, one to see, one to walk. That's worth a moment. Suffering isn't something you abandon; it's something you understand. Craving isn't something you study forever; it's something you set down. Third, why the Buddha says this mattered. In the sutta, he says that until his knowing was clear in all these ways, he didn't claim to be fully awake. Only when he'd walked around every truth did he say it. Fourth, the wheel. The title of the sermon is the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching. A wheel is something you push once and then it rolls. In Theravada lands, the Asalha full moon keeps that first push in memory, and the next day the rains retreat traditionally begins. Each year, the wheel is heard again, and each year, someone hears it as if for the first time.
screen: `FOUR TRUTHS, SHORT.` · `EACH TRUTH, THREE TIMES.` · `UNDERSTAND, LET GO, SEE, WALK.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL TURNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the sermon's outline, if you'd like to say it to yourself, silently, slowly, one line per breath. There is suffering: to be understood. There is a cause: to be let go. There is an ending: to be seen. There is a path: to be walked. Say the four lines once through. Then again, a little slower. Then a third time, and on each line, notice one small, real thing in your own day it might touch. A sore back. A craving for your phone. A moment of quiet. A step you could take. Then let the words go and sit with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Asalha. The full moon that remembers the first sermon in the Deer Park, when the wheel of the teaching was set rolling. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel turns. Today, when something hard comes up, ask which job it needs: understanding, letting go, seeing or a step. Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: On the Asalha full moon, Theravada Buddhists visit temples, listen to or chant the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, keep extra precepts, and often walk around the temple holding candles, flowers and incense.

the gods of the earth shout first, and each heaven above passes it on.

suffering is to be understood. it's craving, the cause, that is to be let go.

he says he didn't claim it until he had walked around every truth.

fork.setup: you've just named four truths. you could stop there. what does the Buddha do in the sutta?
options: moves straight on to the eightfold path.
goes around each truth again: it is to be done, it has been done.
asks the five to vote on whether they agree.
fork.reveal: he walks around each truth three times: this is it, this is its job, this job is done. only then did he claim to be awake.

original.note: Pali: setting in motion the wheel of the teaching, the first sermon's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first sermon is a list of four truths.
what it means: four truths, each walked around three times, each with its own job: understand, let go, see, walk.
what a scholar hears: the three rounds and twelve aspects of Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, and the gods' shout that no one can turn the wheel back.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.6 (the first sermon at Isipatana)

notes: SN 56.11 paraphrased throughout, including the three rounds of each truth (sacca-ñana, kicca-ñana, kata-ñana), the four tasks (pariññeyya, pahatabba, sacchikatabba, bhavetabba), the Buddha not claiming awakening until his knowledge was purified in these ways, and the gods' cry rising through the heavens with the world system trembling and a great light. Confirm.
'Twelve aspects' appears only in the trapdoor's scholar floor; the sutta itself names the three rounds and twelve aspects. Confirm.
'The next day the rains retreat traditionally begins' in Theravada practice; confirm phrasing.
Original: Devanagari of Pali Dhammacakkappavattana; confirm spelling and stress guide.
